entry.title: ZKDP and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2505
entry.content:
ZKDP sought review of a delegate’s refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of his visa after a 7-year-6-month drug trafficking sentence. The Tribunal found he did not pass the character test but nevertheless set aside the refusal and substituted revocation after applying Direction No. 110. It weighed community protection against ties, rehabilitation, pending charges and other factors in a fact-specific decision.

Key holding: Under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), a mandatory cancellation may be revoked where the required representations have been made and the decision-maker is satisfied that there is another reason why the original decision should be revoked.

Under s 501CA(4) of the Act, the Minister may revoke the original decision to cancel if the person makes representations in accordance with the invitation and the Minister is satisfied that the person passes the character test or there is another reason why the original decision should be revoked.

entry.title: Yang and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Citizenship) [2026] ARTA 2501
entry.content:
This was a review of a delegate’s refusal to approve Australian citizenship by descent under s 17(1A) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth), because the delegate was not satisfied the applicant had an Australian citizen parent at the time of her birth under s 16(2)(a). The Tribunal affirmed the refusal after finding the documentary evidence unreliable or insufficient and the claimed parent-child relationship with Mr Yang not established at birth.

Key holding: For the purposes of s 16(2)(a) of the Citizenship Act, a claimed parent-child relationship, whether biological or non-biological, must be shown to have existed at the time of the child’s birth and cannot be established by a later relationship.

Hence, in considering whether the Applicant may be the non-biological child of an Australian citizen parent, the relationship must have existed at the time of the birth of the child. The relationship cannot be developed at a later stage.

entry.title: Roseingrave v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1602
entry.content:
The Federal Court reviewed a Tribunal decision affirming the non-revocation of Mr Roseingrave’s visa cancellation. The Court upheld two grounds because the Tribunal treated Direction 110’s cll 8.3 and 8.4 as exhaustive and failed to evaluate his representations about the impact on his wife and son. The third ground concerning asserted Torres Strait ties failed.

Key holding: The limits of the primary considerations in Direction 110 do not relieve the Tribunal of its obligation to identify, understand and evaluate the representations made by a visa cancellation review applicant.

The correct identification of the limits of the primary considerations referred to in Direction 110 did not relieve the Tribunal of its obligation to identify, understand and evaluate the representations made by Mr Roseingrave.

entry.title: Merhi and Tax Practitioners Board (Taxation and business) [2026] ARTA 2456
entry.content:
The Tribunal affirmed the Tax Practitioners Board’s decision to terminate Mr Merhi’s tax agent registration and impose a five-year period during which he cannot apply for registration. The decision turned on breaches of the Code of Professional Conduct and a finding that he was no longer a fit and proper person, with the Applicant’s failure to give evidence or contradict ASIC/liquidator material being significant.

Key holding: A registered tax agent bears the onus of establishing, on the balance of probabilities and having regard to the seriousness of the matters raised, that he or she remains a fit and proper person.

The onus of proof in establishing fitness and propriety rests with the tax practitioner. It is up to the tax practitioner to establish, and the Tribunal must be reasonably satisfied, that on the balance of probabilities and having regard to the seriousness of the matters raised that the tax practitioner or relevant individual is a fit and proper person.

entry.title: DXJL and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2436
entry.content:
DXJL, the holder of a Global Special Humanitarian (Class XB) (Subclass 202) visa, had his visa mandatorily cancelled and a delegate refused to revoke that cancellation. The Administrative Review Tribunal affirmed the non-revocation decision, finding he did not pass the character test and that Direction No. 110 considerations did not justify revocation.

Key holding: Youth Court offences initially dealt with without conviction may be taken into account in a Direction 110 character assessment where they are later re-sentenced with convictions and detention.

I am therefore satisfied that respective convictions were recorded for each of these 29 offences and that all of them can be taken into account for present purposes.

entry.title: Gates-Pilcher and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Citizenship) [2026] ARTA 2500
entry.content:
This case concerned an application for Australian citizenship by descent by a New Zealand citizen with serious violent offending and non-disclosure of his criminal record. The Tribunal was not positively satisfied that he met the good character criterion and affirmed the refusal.

Key holding: For citizenship by descent under s 16(2)(c) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth), the Tribunal must be positively satisfied that the applicant is of good character at the time of decision; if not, the application cannot be approved.

The Tribunal notes that the good character test does not require it to form an adverse view of the Applicant's character. Rather, it must be positively persuaded or positively satisfied that the Applicant is of good character.

entry.title: Australian Securities and Investments Commission v Dawson [2026] FCA 1548
entry.content:
SXHR, a Sri Lankan unauthorised maritime arrival in immigration detention, sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Bridging E visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal had applied Direction No 110 and refused the visa notwithstanding the applicant’s outstanding Ministerial intervention request. The Federal Court dismissed the review.

Key holding: Direction 110 requires comparison of the risk attached to refusal and grant of the visa, but not separate assessment of every possible outcome after grant where only the grant creates a risk of the applicant remaining in the community.

There is no error in that approach; nothing could have been gained by comparing the nature or extent of that risk depending on which of the two identified scenarios following the grant of a visa eventuated. DVRL does not say anything against that.

entry.title: Xi and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2397
entry.content:
The applicant, a Chinese national, had his Resident Return (Class BB) (Subclass 155) visa mandatorily cancelled under s 501(3A) after being sentenced to 48 months’ imprisonment for offences arising from a cybercrime scam syndicate and firearm possession. A delegate refused to revoke the cancellation under s 501CA(4), and the Tribunal affirmed that decision. The Tribunal found the offending serious and that community protection and expectations outweighed a low risk of reoffending and the applicant’s ties.

Key holding: Serious offending may cause the community expectations consideration under Direction No 110 to weigh significantly against revocation despite an applicant’s personal circumstances.

In the present case, the Tribunal has found the applicant's offending is serious. Taking into consideration the personal circumstances of the applicant, it considers this consideration weighs significantly against revocation of the cancellation.

entry.title: Hoang and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2396
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed the Minister’s refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Hoang’s Class BF Transitional (Permanent) visa under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). Although Mr Hoang had a substantial criminal record for repeat drug and weapons offending and failed the character test, the Tribunal found another reason to revoke under s 501CA(4) and set aside the refusal.

Key holding: A residual risk of reoffending may be acceptable, and another reason to revoke may exist, where serious addiction-related offending is offset by sustained rehabilitation, family support and long residence.

The Applicant has, nonetheless, made significant progress in rehabilitation and has retained the support and trust of his immediate family who are an important element to his future success. I consider that the 'residual' risk of reoffending is acceptable despite the potentially serious consequences for the community, and Mr Hoang's length of residence from a young age must take into account.

entry.title: Mishra and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2327
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s decision not to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Mishra’s Subclass 155 Five-Year Resident Return visa under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). Mr Mishra accepted he did not pass the character test because of a 22-month aggregate sentence for family violence offences. The Tribunal affirmed the non-revocation decision after considering whether another reason existed under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii) and Direction No. 110.

Key holding: Where a visa is mandatorily cancelled because the holder fails the character test due to a substantial criminal record, the Tribunal must consider whether there is another reason to revoke under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii), applying Direction No. 110.

In accordance with s 501CA(4)(b)(ii), the Tribunal must therefore consider whether there is another reason to exercise the discretion under s 501CA(4) to revoke the original decision.

entry.title: Mohamedali v Assistant Minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 1531
entry.content:
The Federal Court allowed a consent judicial review application concerning a decision by the Assistant Minister under s 501BA of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to cancel the applicant’s visa. The Assistant Minister conceded jurisdictional error because he failed to consider an updated psychologist’s report that was constructively before him and relevant to the applicant’s risk of reoffending. The Court made orders quashing the cancellation decision.

Key holding: A s 501BA decision is affected by jurisdictional error if the Minister fails to properly consider material constructively before him that is relevant to the risk the applicant poses to the Australian community and the national interest.

Accordingly, the Assistant Minister accepts that his decision was affected by jurisdictional error as a result of his failure to properly consider the risk the applicant posed to the Australian community.

entry.title: Smith v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1520
entry.content:
Mr Smith, a New Zealand citizen, had his Class TY Subclass 444 visa cancelled under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) after criminal convictions and imprisonment. A delegate refused to revoke the cancellation, and the Administrative Review Tribunal affirmed that refusal. On judicial review, the Federal Court found the Tribunal misconstrued Direction 110’s definition of “family violence” and set aside its decision.

Key holding: Conduct falling within an example of family violence in Direction 110 cl 4 is not automatically family violence; it must also have the effect of coercing or controlling a family member or causing that person to be fearful.

For example, behaviour which involves "intentionally damaging or destroying property" will not necessarily constitute family violence. It will only do so if that behaviour had the effect of coercing or controlling a member of the perpetrator's family, or causing the family member or members to be fearful.

entry.title: Huseni and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Citizenship) [2026] ARTA 2420
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a refusal of Australian citizenship by conferral on good character grounds under s 21(2)(h) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth). The Minister alleged the applicant failed to declare alternative names and provided undeclared migration assistance through his company, Immi Solution. The Tribunal found no dishonest intent and no proven personal provision of immigration assistance, and was satisfied the applicant was of good character.

Key holding: For s 21(2)(h), good character requires a holistic assessment of enduring moral qualities and is not negated by every acknowledged mistake or oversight, particularly where there is no fraud or dishonesty.

His actions, when considered on an individual or cumulative basis, are regrettable but do not reach the threshold of being demonstrative of someone who is presently not of good character.

entry.title: Niven and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2274
entry.content:
This was a merits review of a delegate’s decision not to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Niven’s Class TY Subclass 444 Special Category (Temporary) visa under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal found the applicant did not pass the character test but accepted there was another reason to revoke the cancellation, set aside the delegate’s decision, and substituted a decision revoking the cancellation.

Key holding: Under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii), where an applicant fails the character test, the Tribunal may revoke mandatory cancellation if satisfied there is another reason, applying Direction no. 110.

Section 501CA(4) states that the Minister may revoke the original decision if: (a) the person makes representations in accordance with the invitation; and (b) the Minister is satisfied: (i) that the person passes the character test (as defined by s 501); or (ii) that there is another reason why the original decision should be revoked.

entry.title: Upson and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2275
entry.content:
In Upson and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2275, a 31-year-old New Zealand citizen who has lived in Australia since infancy had his special category visa mandatorily cancelled under s 501(3A) after being sentenced to 7 years 6 months for serious drug offences. A delegate refused to revoke the cancellation, but the Administrative Review Tribunal set that decision aside and substituted revocation after finding “another reason” under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii).

Key holding: Under Direction no. 110, whether a non-citizen poses an “unacceptable risk” is a distinct evaluative conclusion reached by balancing the likelihood and potential harm of future offending, not merely the likelihood of re-offending.

The concept of 'risk', and whether it is 'unacceptable', under cl 8.1.2(1) of the Direction is not the same thing as the 'likelihood of the non-citizen engaging in further criminal or other serious conduct'.[25]

entry.title: Nyagua and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2298
entry.content:
This Tribunal review concerns the mandatory cancellation of Ms Nyagua’s Resident Return (Subclass 155) visa after her conviction for importing a marketable quantity of a border-controlled drug. Although she failed the character test, the Tribunal found another reason to revoke the cancellation. The decision under review was set aside and the visa cancellation revoked under s 501CA(4).

Key holding: Where a non-citizen fails the character test after mandatory visa cancellation, the Tribunal may revoke cancellation under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii) if satisfied there is another reason, exercising the discretion in accordance with the applicable ministerial direction.

Section 501CA(4)(b)(ii) of the Act requires the Tribunal to consider if there is another reason why the discretion should be exercised to revoke the original decision. In exercising this discretion, the Tribunal must have regard to the Direction (s 499(2A)).

entry.title: Majak and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2277
entry.content:
Majak sought review of a delegate’s decision not to revoke the mandatory cancellation of his Class XB Subclass 202 visa under s 501(3A) after serious assault convictions. The Tribunal accepted he failed the character test but found “another reason” to revoke under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii), principally the best interests of his infant daughter and the extreme impediments if removed to South Sudan. It set aside the delegate’s decision and substituted revocation.

Key holding: Where the Tribunal is satisfied on the evidence that another reason exists, it should set aside the non-revocation decision and substitute revocation under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii).

Having reached this conclusion, I find that there is 'another reason' for the revocation of the cancellation decision for the purposes of section 501CA(4)(b)(ii) of the Act. Accordingly, it is appropriate for me to set aside the decision under review and substitute decision that the cancellation decision be revoked.

entry.title: Ututaonga and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2285
entry.content:
This is a migration review of a delegate’s decision not to revoke the mandatory cancellation of a New Zealand citizen’s Class TY Subclass 444 Special Category (Temporary) visa under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The applicant had a substantial criminal record, including serious drug supply offences, and the Tribunal had to weigh the Direction no. 110 considerations for and against revocation.

Key holding: In exercising the s 501CA(4) discretion, the Tribunal must weigh all primary and other considerations under Direction no. 110 in a single evaluation, with greater weight generally given to protection of the Australian community.

In determining the weight to be applied to each consideration, the Tribunal considered the primary and other considerations and weighed them in light of the evidence and findings using the guidance provided by the Direction. Greater weight must generally be given to the protection of the Australian community than other primary considerations.

entry.title: ROBB and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2279
entry.content:
The Tribunal affirmed a delegate’s decision not to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Robb’s subclass 155 visa under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). Mr Robb accepted he failed the character test because of a substantial criminal record, and the Tribunal found the protection of the Australian community, family violence and community expectations outweighed his ties and rehabilitation claims. Key holding: Where an applicant fails the character test, the Tribunal can revoke a mandatory visa cancellation only if satisfied under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii) that there is another reason, assessed through Direction No. 110.

The statutory power to revoke will only be enlivened if there is 'another reason' why the Cancellation Decision should be revoked.

entry.title: 2635010 (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2284
entry.content:
The Tribunal refused a Bridging E (Class WE) Subclass 050 visa to an Iranian applicant in immigration detention after criminal convictions and prior protection visa refusal. The applicant relied on a pending s 48B ministerial intervention request and asserted he had acceptable arrangements to depart Australia if those avenues failed. The Tribunal affirmed the delegate’s refusal.

Key holding: A Bridging E visa applicant does not satisfy cl 050.212(5B) where they have previously made any s 48B ministerial intervention request, even if the earlier request was finalised as not considered and a later request is treated as non-repeat under the Ministerial Instructions; the Tribunal cannot read the Ministerial Instructions exception into the regulation.

It finds that to conclude for the purposes of cl 050.212(5B) that the applicant's 23 December 2025 request is not a repeat request on the basis of the Ministerial Instructions is to read into cl 050.212(5B) a set of circumstances and provisions that the clause does not contemplate or provide for.

entry.title: 2609101 (Refugee) [2026] ARTA 2316
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s refusal of a Protection visa to a Dinka man raised in Australia, who feared removal to South Sudan and [Country 1]. It accepted he was a South Sudanese national and found a well-founded fear of persecution in South Sudan by reason of ethnicity, imputed political opinion and particular social group. The Tribunal set aside the refusal and remitted the matter with an order that he is a refugee under s 5H(1) of the Migration Act.

Key holding: A person involuntarily returned to South Sudan with mental illness and no family or community support may be recognised as a refugee as a member of a particular social group facing systematic discrimination and a real risk of detention and ill-treatment.

I am satisfied that the applicant, as a person with mental illness being returned involuntarily to South Sudan without any family or community support, falls within a particular social group of persons with mental illness in South Sudan who face systematic discrimination and a real risk of detention and ill-treatment.

entry.title: So v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 345 (26 March 2026)
entry.content:
The Federal Court reviewed an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming non-revocation of the applicant’s mandatorily cancelled Resident Return visa under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act. The Tribunal found the applicant failed the character test and that there was no another reason to revoke, but the Court held it failed to consider his non-refoulement claims as required by Ministerial Direction 110. The decision was set aside and remitted for redetermination.

Key holding: A decision-maker considering revocation under s 501CA(4) must consider claims capable of engaging international non-refoulement obligations raised by a non-citizen not subject to a protection finding, as required by para 9.1.2(1) of Direction 110.

Paragraph 9.1.2(1) of Direction 110 expressly requires that claims raised by a non-citizen who is not the subject of a protection finding that may give rise to international non-refoulement obligations "must be considered". The provision recognises that a person may raise international non-refoulement obligations distinct from the statutory "protection obligations" assessed in the protection visa process.

Verbatim excerpt, AI-selected. Check the full text.

Federal Court of Australia, 26 Mar 2026, [2026] FCA 345

entry.title: Fraser v Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 336 (25 March 2026)
entry.content:
Mr Fraser, a Canadian citizen, had his visa cancelled under s 501(3A) after a 4-year sentence; the ART later revoked that cancellation. In July 2025 the Assistant Minister set aside the ART decision and cancelled the visa under s 501BA. Mr Fraser’s judicial review alleged jurisdictional error in failing to engage with evidence about Ms Bannister’s children and in failing to consider s 501E; the Federal Court dismissed the application.

Key holding: The s 501E bar is a direct and immediate legal consequence of the Minister exercising the s 501BA power, so the legal-consequences principle applies to it.

Therefore, respectfully to those who have expressed a different view, I would characterise the legal consequence of the exercise of the discretion conferred by s 501BA that I have described as direct and immediate. Consequently, it was a legal consequence to which the principle relied upon by Mr Fraser applied.

entry.title: RRRB v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 337 (25 March 2026)
entry.content:
RRRB sought judicial review of an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming the non-revocation of his visa cancellation under the Migration Act. The Tribunal found he did not pass the character test due to a serious drug conviction and that there was not “another reason” to revoke. The Federal Court dismissed the application.

Key holding: The list of specified conduct in cl 8.5(2)(a)-(f) of Ministerial Direction 110 is not exhaustive so as to prevent the Tribunal from considering other serious offending when applying the general community expectation in cl 8.5(1) and the first sentence of cl 8.5(2).

However, the list should not be regarded as "exhaustive" in the sense of preventing the Tribunal from having regard to other kinds of offending when considering whether the first sentence of cl 8.5(2) is relevant in the particular case before it.

entry.content:

entry.title: Pillay v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCAFC 24 (19 March 2026)
entry.content:
The Full Court considered an appeal from judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming non-revocation of Mr Pillay’s visa cancellation under the Migration Act. The Tribunal’s adverse credit findings relied on an allegedly wrong premise that Mr Pillay had withheld documents from a psychologist, and it also declined to give weight to Australian business interests under Direction 99. The Full Court allowed the appeal, quashed the Tribunal decision and remitted the review.

Key holding: A tribunal may commit jurisdictional error by constructively failing to review if it fails to make an obvious inquiry into a critical fact that is easily ascertained and that failure has a sufficient link to the outcome.

It may be that a failure to make an obvious inquiry about a critical fact, the existence of which is easily ascertained, could, in some circumstances, supply a sufficient link to the outcome to constitute a failure to review. If so, such a failure could give rise to jurisdictional error by constructive failure to exercise jurisdiction.

Federal Court of Australia (Full Court), 19 Mar 2026, [2026] FCAFC 24

entry.title: HLWS v Minister for Immigration and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 243 (12 March 2026)
entry.content:
HLWS sought an extension of time and judicial review of an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Resolution of Status visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal accepted a psychologist’s low/moderate reoffending risk assessed “without intervention” but did not address HLWS’s willingness to undertake interventions. The Federal Court granted the extension and allowed review, finding a material jurisdictional error.

Key holding: A tribunal commits jurisdictional error where it overlooks a substantial and clearly articulated contention that is material to its statutory risk assessment, such that the outcome could realistically have been different.

Accordingly, in my view, in failing to consider the interventions point at all, the Tribunal failed to discharge the task and function accorded to it by Parliament, and engaged in jurisdictional error.

entry.title: Kamara and Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs (Citizenship) [2024] AATA 3560
entry.content:
The Applicant sought review of a delegate’s decision refusing his citizenship by conferral application because the delegate was not satisfied he was of good character under s 21(2)(h) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth). The Tribunal found the Applicant was of good character despite historical offending, a 2016 drink-driving offence, traffic infringements and disclosure issues. It remitted the matter with a direction that he satisfies s 21(2)(h).

Key holding: The good character criterion in s 21(2)(h) requires a broad moral assessment against the moral norms of the Australian community, rather than a purely conviction-based test.

The character test is ultimately a moral test, and morality can only be tested within the confines of moral norms in society.

entry.title: Rangiuia and Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs (Migration) [2024] AATA 3550
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed the cancellation of Mr Rangiuia’s Class TY Subclass 444 Special Category (Temporary) visa under s 501(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). He conceded that he did not pass the character test under s 501(6)(b) because of his membership of the Mongrel Mob and Bandidos outlaw motorcycle gangs. The Tribunal affirmed cancellation, finding protection of the Australian community and serious family violence outweighed his ties to Australia and the best interests of his children.

Key holding: Once a non-citizen fails the character test, the Tribunal’s remaining task is to exercise the s 501(2) cancellation discretion in accordance with Direction No. 110.

Having failed the character test, the issue for the Tribunal is whether to exercise the discretion to cancel the visa, guided by the considerations set out in Direction 110.

entry.title: SRFX and Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs (Citizenship) [2024] AATA 3549
entry.content:
SRFX applied for Australian citizenship by conferral, but a delegate refused approval under s 24(1) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth), finding he did not satisfy the good character requirement in s 21(2)(h) and that his identity could not be established under s 24(3). The Tribunal reviewed the decision, relying on the applicant’s migration history, prior partner visa findings and allegedly bogus documents, and affirmed the refusal. The case turns on whether the Tribunal could be satisfied of his good character and identity.

Key holding: In assessing good character for citizenship, the decision-maker must make a holistic assessment of the person’s enduring moral qualities, and a single sufficiently serious adverse incident can outweigh otherwise good qualities.

The decision-maker must look holistically at applicant's behaviour over time and reach a conclusion about the person's enduring moral qualities. Notwithstanding the obligation to take a holistic approach, it is established that a single adverse incident of sufficient weight and seriousness can outweigh many good qualities in a person.

entry.title: Verrill and Minister for Immigration and Multicultural Affairs (Migration) [2024] AATA 3509
entry.content:
David Verrill asked the Administrative Appeals Tribunal to disqualify Senior Member R Bellamy from his remitted review of a visa cancellation under s 501 of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). He alleged actual and apprehended bias arising from adverse media about an unrelated decision, criticisms of his former lawyers, a prior decision concerning another non-citizen, and the allocation of other cases to the member. That test is whether a fair-minded lay observer might reasonably apprehend that a judge might not bring an impartial mind to the resolution of the question the judge is required to decide.

entry.title: Baggaley (Migration) [2024] AATA 3839
entry.content:
This Tribunal review concerns cancellation of a Subclass 801 (Spouse) visa after the applicant failed to notify the Department that her de facto relationship with her sponsor had ceased before her permanent partner visa was granted. The Tribunal found the s 107 notice valid, the s 104 non-compliance established, and affirmed cancellation on discretionary grounds.

Key holding: In exercising the s 109 cancellation discretion, non-compliance that goes to the central criterion for visa eligibility is given very substantial weight and may outweigh hardship and community contribution factors.

However, weighing the matter as a whole, it gives very substantial weight to the fact that the non-compliance identified went to the central criterion for eligibility for the visa that the subject of this application. This is a matter going to the integrity of the Partner visa program, and the Tribunal is satisfied that the considerations in favour of cancellation outweigh those advanced to the contrary.

entry.title: Hughes and Minister for Immigration, Citizenship, and Multicultural Affairs (Migration) [2024] AATA 3158
entry.content:
Michael Hughes, a 58-year-old New Zealand/United Kingdom citizen, had his subclass 189 visa mandatorily cancelled after being convicted of indecent dealing with a child under 13 and sentenced to 20 months’ imprisonment. He sought review of a delegate’s decision not to revoke that cancellation under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal affirmed the non-revocation decision, applying Direction no. 110 and refusing to go behind the conviction and sentence.

Key holding: In a s 501CA review, the Tribunal cannot go behind the essential facts of the conviction and sentence that founded the mandatory cancellation, and an applicant bears a heavy onus to challenge those facts.

In those circumstances, it is not open to the Tribunal to go behind the essential facts of that conviction and sentence. Moreover, the Applicant has not discharged what would otherwise be his "heavy onus" to challenge the facts upon which the conviction and sentence are necessarily based as set out above.

entry.title: Goncalves De Sa (Migration) [2024] AATA 3350
entry.content:
The Tribunal affirmed refusal of Employer Nomination (Permanent) (Class EN) Subclass 186 visas in the Temporary Residence Transition stream because the primary applicant, a chef, could not demonstrate competent English at the time of application. Although he spoke English well at hearing and had substantial culinary experience, his IELTS results and Portuguese passport did not meet the prescribed criteria, and the Tribunal had no discretion.

Key holding: For a Subclass 186 TRT visa, competent English must be established at the time of application through a specified test score or specified passport, failing which cl 186.222(a) is not satisfied and the Tribunal has no discretion.

Since neither 1.15C(1) nor 1.15C(2) are satisfied, 1.15C is not satisfied. As 1.15C is not satisfied, the Tribunal finds the applicant did not have competent English at the time of lodging the visa application, and therefore does not satisfy 186.222(a).

entry.content:
Mr Sio, a New Zealand citizen holding a subclass 444 visa, had his visa mandatorily cancelled under s 501(3A) and a delegate decided not to revoke the cancellation under s 501CA(4). Following the Full Federal Court's decision in Pearson, the cancellation was invalid because an aggregate sentence is not a term of imprisonment of 12 months or more, so the visa was taken not to have been cancelled and the revocation decision was a nullity. The Tribunal held it had no jurisdiction to review the nullity and dismissed the application by consent.

Administrative Review Tribunal, 10 Jan 2023, [2023] AATA 9

entry.title: Hossain v Minister for Immigration and Border Protection [2018] HCA 34
entry.content:
The appellant applied for a partner visa. A delegate of the Minister refused the visa, and the Tribunal affirmed the refusal, finding that the visa application was not made within 28 days and that there were no compelling reasons for not applying that criterion. The Tribunal assessed whether compelling reasons existed as at the time of application rather than at the time of its decision. The High Court dismissed the appeal, holding that this error was not jurisdictional.

High Court of Australia, 15 Aug 2018, [2018] HCA 34

entry.title: Re Minister for Immigration and Multicultural and Indigenous Affairs; Ex parte Akpata [2002] HCA 34
entry.content:
The applicant's parent visa was refused on character grounds under s 501, which by operation of s 501F automatically cancelled his bridging visa and led to his immigration detention. He sought relief in the High Court alleging a denial of procedural fairness in that he was not warned of the cancellation/detention consequences, but the Court held the decision was a privative clause decision under s 474, satisfied the Hickman conditions, and that s 501F created a statutory state of affairs not subject to procedural fairness.

High Court of Australia, 2 Sep 2002, [2002] HCA 34

entry.title: Re Refugee Review Tribunal; Ex parte H [2001] HCA 28
entry.content:
The High Court considered whether the Refugee Review Tribunal's conduct during a hearing gave rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias. The Tribunal repeatedly interrupted and challenged the credibility of the applicants, who were unrepresented. The Court found that a fair-minded lay observer might apprehend bias and granted writs of prohibition, certiorari, and mandamus, quashing the Tribunal's decision and requiring it to redetermine the matter according to law.

High Court of Australia, 24 May 2001, [2001] HCA 28
